title: Rhabdomyolysis (adult)
subject: nephrology
summary: Confirm with CK above 5 times normal, start early isotonic crystalloid titrated to urine output 1 to 3 mL/kg/h (up to 300 mL/h), treat hyperkalaemia, look for compartment syndrome, and avoid routine bicarbonate, mannitol and diuretics.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Diagnosis: CK above 5 times the upper limit of normal or above 1000 U/L, with muscle pain, weakness or swelling. Dark (tea-coloured) urine that is dipstick positive for blood without red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobinuria.

AKI risk rises with CK: about 10% develop kidney failure with CK above 5000 U/L, and CK above 16,000 U/L is more strongly associated. A McMahon score of 6 or more predicts need for dialysis and death.
CK peaks at 24 to 72 hours, so a modest early CK can rise further.

Causes: crush and prolonged immobilisation, compartment syndrome, vascular injury, extreme exertion, seizures, heat stroke, alcohol and drugs (cocaine, statins), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, infections, electrolyte disorders and genetic myopathies.
Indian context: consider leptospirosis, dengue, falciparum malaria and scrub typhus, sea snake envenomation, multiple wasp or hornet stings, heat stroke in outdoor workers, and severe hypokalaemia.

sections.title: Immediate management
items: Start isotonic crystalloid early: 0.9% saline or Ringer lactate are both acceptable. Begin at about 400 mL/h and titrate between 200 and 1000 mL/h.
Target urine output 1 to 3 mL/kg/h, up to 300 mL/h (about 200 to 300 mL/h in most adults), and continue until CK is reliably falling.
Check potassium and ECG immediately and repeat often; treat hyperkalaemia per the Hyperkalaemia protocol (IV calcium for ECG changes, insulin-glucose).

Examine every limb for compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling. Get urgent surgical review for fasciotomy; delay beyond 6 hours risks irreversible muscle damage.
Stop causative drugs (statins and others), cool heat stroke, control seizures and agitation, and treat infection.

sections.title: Investigations
items: CK at presentation and serially (for example daily) until it has peaked and is reliably falling.
Creatinine, potassium, calcium, phosphate, urate, bicarbonate or blood gas, LFTs (AST rises from muscle), CBC and coagulation profile for DIC.
Urine dipstick and microscopy, and 12-lead ECG.
Cause-directed tests: drug and toxicology screen, TSH, tropical fever work-up, and metabolic myopathy testing if episodes recur or follow mild exertion.

sections.title: Supportive care
items: Do not routinely give sodium bicarbonate or mannitol: they have not reduced AKI or dialysis. Avoid loop diuretics except for fluid overload.
Treat early hypocalcaemia only if symptomatic or with severe hyperkalaemia; calcium given early deposits in injured muscle, and rebound hypercalcaemia can occur in the recovery phase.
Hyperphosphataemia is common: avoid calcium supplements that increase calcium phosphate deposition.
If oliguric AKI develops, stop escalating fluids, reassess volume, and prepare for dialysis rather than pushing fluid into an anuric patient.

sections.title: Escalate
items: Dialysis for standard indications: refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemia. There is no role for dialysis to prevent AKI.
HDU or ICU for rapidly rising CK with AKI, hyperkalaemia, crush injury, compartment syndrome, or McMahon score 6 or more.
Crush injury in a mass casualty setting: early fluids and triage to a centre with dialysis capacity.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Hourly urine output (catheter), fluid balance and daily weight; examine for pulmonary oedema, especially in older adults and heart failure.
Potassium frequently in the first 24 to 48 hours (every 4 to 6 hours in severe cases), with creatinine, calcium and phosphate at least daily.
Repeat limb checks for evolving compartment syndrome, particularly in sedated, intoxicated or intubated patients.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing compartment syndrome in patients who cannot report pain.
Stopping monitoring after one CK value before the peak.
Fluid overload from fixed high-rate fluids in oliguric AKI or heart failure.
Routine bicarbonate causing alkalosis and worsening ionised hypocalcaemia.

drugs.name: Isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or Ringer lactate)
drugs.dose: Start about 400 mL/h IV, titrate 200 to 1000 mL/h to urine output 1 to 3 mL/kg/h (up to 300 mL/h)
drugs.notes: Continue until CK is reliably falling; reduce if overload or oliguric AKI.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10%
drugs.notes: Only for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes or symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

drugs.name: Soluble insulin with glucose
drugs.dose: 10 units soluble insulin IV with 25 g glucose
drugs.notes: Hyperkalaemia; monitor glucose for 6 hours (see Hyperkalaemia protocol).
